questions.question: Explain what is meant by balance in an ecosystem, using the impala and lion populations of a reserve, and name four limiting factors that keep populations within limits.
questions.expected_answer: Balance is dynamic: populations rise and fall but the changes correct themselves. More grass → more impala → more lions a year or two later → fewer impala → fewer lions → impala recover; the predator peak lags the prey peak and neither reaches zero. Limiting factors: food, water, space/shelter, predators, disease and parasites, competition (any four). The largest population an area can support long term is its carrying capacity.

questions.question: Compare natural and human disruptions of ecosystems, giving two South African examples of each and stating the key difference in how ecosystems respond.
questions.expected_answer: Natural: drought (e.g. Kruger 2015–16 hippo and buffalo deaths), floods, fire (necessary in fynbos/grassland at the right frequency), disease (rinderpest 1890s). Human: habitat destruction (Highveld grassland ploughed, Cape Flats built over), pollution (Vaal/Hartbeespoort algal blooms, acid mine drainage), overharvesting (perlemoen, rhino poaching), overgrazing and erosion, alien invasive species, climate change (Cape Town Day Zero drought). Natural disruptions are usually temporary and followed by recovery; human ones are larger, continuous or permanent.

questions.question: Define alien and invasive species and explain why invaders succeed. Then apply the five-step case study method to water hyacinth on Hartbeespoort Dam.
questions.expected_answer: Alien: introduced to a region where it did not occur naturally; invasive: an alien that spreads and causes harm. They succeed because they have left behind their natural predators, parasites and competitors, and local organisms are not adapted to control them. Case study: (1) human disruption, alien species; (2) covers the surface and blocks light, so submerged plants die, and rotting hyacinth strips oxygen; (3) fish and other animals die, food web collapses; (4) anglers lose fish, irrigation pumps and boats are blocked; (5) mechanical removal plus a biological control weevil that feeds only on hyacinth, because herbicides would poison the dam.
